summary:
This project was born out of the growing concern over global soil degradation. According to the UNCCD, up to 90% of the Earth's soils could be degraded by 2050.

In an increasingly dynamic and rapidly changing environment, traditional prediction methods are no longer sufficient to accurately anticipate agricultural productivity. To address this challenge, we have developed a Dynamic Crop Yield Prediction Model, combining historical crop productivity data with real-time soil quality measurements to identify the crops with the highest expected economic return.

We envision this project as an open-source initiative, encouraging global collaboration and the collection of as much soil data as possible from different regions around the world. By leveraging this growing dataset, we aim to develop increasingly accurate models capable of predicting soil quality, supporting sustainable agricultural decisions, and ultimately helping prevent further soil degradation.
details:
Plot Advisor - From orbit to the furrow: what to plant, where, and when.

Plot Advisor is a low-cost IoT and machine-learning platform that tells farmers which crop best fits each part of their land. It combines a mesh of solar-ready ESP32 sensor beacons placed in the field with a crop-suitability model trained on 15 years of NASA POWER climate data and real European harvest statistics. The farm is split into zones that behave differently, and each zone gets a ranked list of crops, with expected yield, local market price and whether it is sowing season right now.

How it works

  1. In the field: ESP32 beacons measure air temperature and humidity, light, soil moisture, conductivity, temperature and pH. Some use their own probes; others read Xiaomi MiFlora sensors over Bluetooth LE. The beacons form a self-healing painlessMesh network, so only one bridge node needs Wi-Fi. That bridge publishes every reading over MQTT to a Raspberry Pi gateway at the farm. What is a mesh? A mesh network is a decentralized system where devices (nodes) connect directly and cooperatively to one another. Instead of every device needing to reach a central router (like traditional Wi-Fi), nodes can relay data hopping from one device to the next until it reaches the destination. This means areas with no internet available could still deploy and run it autonomously, requiring internet access only at the main gateway node. In the real implementation, either a single battery or a solar panel for each beacon would be used. To increase maximum distance between nodes, a LoRa module would be used. A full-equiped beacon would have a cost of around 65€. The breakdown of this cost, with additional information about the project can be found in the README of our "Global" repository.

(different beacons we used to create the actual mesh)

  1. At the gateway: Mosquitto, Telegraf and InfluxDB store the time series, and PostgreSQL holds the farm layout. Icinga 2 and Grafana monitor every beacon and send instant phone alerts when one goes offline.
  2. Zoning: a spatial clustering algorithm (SKATER on a minimum spanning tree of the beacons) groups neighbouring beacons with similar soil and microclimate into management zones.
  3. Recommendation: for each zone we build the same 14 features the model was trained on: seasonal temperature and rainfall, radiation, humidity, soil moisture and pH. The values come from the beacons and from Meteomatics weather data. Two gradient-boosting models predict (a) the share of land that regions with that climate devote to each crop, and (b) the expected yield. Crops are ranked by that share, adjusted for how much better the crop yields and sells here than the European average. The ranking is never by gross revenue, because that would always favour the same expensive crops. Training info and the models can be found at our backend repository.
  4. The dashboard: a web map over satellite imagery shows every beacon, the mesh links, live readings and the coloured zones with their best crop. Number of zones and preferred type of crops can be selected.

(example of a dashboard workflow)

The complete rundown of the architecture we used for the actual demo can be found here:

NASA data

  • NASA POWER (Agroclimatology community) is the backbone of the model. Monthly T2M, PRECTOTCORR, ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN, RH2M and GWETROOT (root-zone soil wetness) for about 250 European NUTS-2 regions from 2010 to 2024.
  • These are joined with Eurostat regional crop areas and yields, and with ISRIC SoilGrids soil pH, giving roughly 59,000 region-year-crop records and 18 field crops.
  • On regions the model never saw during training, the region's real main crop appears in its top 2 in 79% of cases.

Benefits and impact

  • Smallholders get agronomic advice that used to require expensive consultants, from hardware costing a few euros per beacon.
  • Healthier rotations and soil resilience: Planting crops matched to each micro-zone's soil and water profile reduces failed harvests, curbs wasted water and fertilizer, and supports diverse rotations that interrupt pest cycles and prevent nutrient depletion.
  • Tailored to farmer priorities: Rather than forcing one metric, farmers can weigh recommendations against their own operational goals-whether conserving water, improving soil organic matter, producing forage, or maximizing local market value.
  • It is an adaptation tool: retrained on new NASA POWER years, it shows how climate change shifts which crops make sense on each plot.
  • We validated the full pipeline on four very different farms: a live prototype farm with four real boards, plus three simulated farms built on real field boundaries and weather in Aragon (Spain), Wexford (Ireland) and Romerike (Norway). The recommendations change sensibly: durum wheat and barley in dry Spain, wheat and silage maize in Ireland, wheat, barley and oilseed rape in Norway.

(example of our system actually physically working and retrieving data from the flowerpots in the hackathon)

  • Completely open source. We believe the best way to maximize this technology's impact is by allowing the community to nurture and collaborate on it-growing the network and expanding our datasets to continuously improve our models.
    A full guide to deploy the project with docker is available in the repositories below.
  • Exhaustive monitoring: we put a big focus on infrastructure and monitoring. All data regarding system storage and availability is logged. When a beacon fails, we receive an SMS warning thanks to Icinga 2.


    (examples of our monitoring system in action)

Why it is creative

  • Most precision-agriculture products either read sensors or show satellite maps. Plot Advisor connects the two scales: global NASA climate records teach the model what grows where, and a cheap mesh of field sensors tells it what this particular corner of this particular farm looks like. It also answers the question farmers really ask, "what should I plant here?", per zone and per season, instead of only showing graphs.
  • It is also important to note that thanks to the mesh, the infrastructure becomes really resilient and a few beacons can fail without compromising the entire system.
  • Farms rarely have uniform soil or moisture. By running spatial clustering (SKATER on a minimum spanning tree) over the sensor mesh, Plot Advisor automatically discovers natural management zones.
  • Our way to rank profit is also well thought out: Standard profit-based algorithms fail in agriculture because they always recommend the most expensive cash crop regardless of risk or input costs. By ranking crops using regional climate suitability × local yield advantage, our system surfaces resilient, realistic rotation options tailored to the land rather than chasing artificial market hype.

Factors we considered

  • Honest data: no synthetic training data. Our first model, trained on a popular synthetic dataset, recommended sugarcane everywhere, so we rebuilt it on real public sources.
  • No revenue bias: we rank by share × advantage rather than revenue, since no public source gives per-crop costs.
  • Rural connectivity: a mesh network with a single uplink, and local storage at the gateway.
  • Reliability: per-node monitoring and alerts.
  • Multi-farm design: separate data and login for each client.
  • Explainability: every recommendation shows its share, yield, price and sowing window.
  • Modular and interchangeable. Beacons and the InfluxDB workflow can be used alone, even without internet access.
  • A paid plan would also be available, where we host all the services in a multi-tenant infrastructure and offer support.

Future Lines of Development

  • Soil Health & Rotation Predictive Modeling: Integrating a dedicated soil health and status prediction model into the pipeline to evaluate which crops best preserve or restore soil over multi-year cycles. This model will be continuously trained using the real-time telemetry data gathered by our active deployments.
  • LoRa-Powered Long-Range Mesh: Upgrading the beacon mesh with LoRa modules to ensure robust communication across vast, expansive crop fields (hardware costs are already factored into our economic estimates).
  • AWS Serverless Cloud Architecture: Scaling the platform with a fully designed, production-ready serverless cloud infrastructure on AWS. This infrastructure hosted in AWS, would follow a similar diagram to this:

Tools and technologies

  • Hardware: ESP32 (Arduino, painlessMesh, NimBLE), MiFlora BLE sensors, DHT11, analog light, soil and pH probes, Raspberry Pi.
  • Gateway and data: Mosquitto MQTT, Telegraf, InfluxDB, PostgreSQL, Icinga 2, Grafana, ntfy, Docker.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, scikit-learn (gradient boosting), pandas, GeoPandas, rasterio.
  • Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, Esri satellite imagery.
  • Data sources: NASA POWER, Eurostat, ISRIC SoilGrids, Meteomatics, GGCMI Phase 3 crop calendar, OpenStreetMap, SIGPAC (Spain), NIBIO AR5 (Norway).
  • Model training: Google Colab.
